theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Power in AC Circuits

Multiplying v = √2 V sin ωt by i = √2 I sin(ωt − φ) and using 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B) gives the expression below. The first term is constant; the second oscillates at 2ω and averages to zero over a cycle, so the average power is VI cos φ. Whenever φ is not zero, p goes negative for part of each cycle, which is the moment the inductor or capacitor hands stored energy back to the source.

theoryAdd.plainText: p(t) = VI cos φ − VI cos(2ωt − φ)

theoryAdd.text: Complex power combines all three powers in one phasor: S = V I*, where I* is the conjugate of the current phasor. Its real part is P and its imaginary part is Q, with Q positive for an inductive load and negative for a capacitive one. The conjugate is essential; multiplying V by I directly gives the wrong angle. In terms of the load elements, P = I²R = V_R²/R and Q = I²X = V_X²/X.

theoryAdd.latex: S = V I^{*} = P + jQ, \qquad |S| = VI
theoryAdd.plainText: S = V × conj(I) = P + jQ; |S| = VI

theoryAdd.text: When several loads share a supply, complex power is conserved: the total P is the sum of the individual P values and the total Q is the algebraic sum of the Q values, with capacitive VAR counted as negative. The individual kVA figures do not simply add unless all loads have the same power factor. This is the basis of every power-factor correction calculation: the capacitor adds negative Q while leaving P untouched.

theoryAdd.plainText: Line loss ratio = (cos φ1 / cos φ2)², for the same P and V

theoryAdd.text:
Example 1: 230 V supply; heater 2 kW (pf 1) + motor 3 kW at 0.75 lagging
Motor: tan φ = tan(cos⁻¹ 0.75) = 0.882, Q = 3 × 0.882 = 2.65 kVAR
Total P = 2 + 3 = 5 kW
Total Q = 0 + 2.65 = 2.65 kVAR (lagging)
S = √(5² + 2.65²) = 5.66 kVA (not 2 + 4 = 6 kVA)
Overall pf = 5/5.66 = 0.884 lagging
Line current = 5660/230 = 24.6 A

Example 2: 40 kW, 400 V, 50 Hz single-phase load, pf 0.7 -> 0.95 lagging
tan φ1 = tan(cos⁻¹ 0.7) = 1.020, tan φ2 = tan(cos⁻¹ 0.95) = 0.329
Q_C = 40 × (1.020 − 0.329) = 27.7 kVAR
C = Q_C/(2πfV²) = 27 660/(2π × 50 × 400²) = 550 µF
Current before = 40 000/(400 × 0.7) = 142.9 A
Current after = 40 000/(400 × 0.95) = 105.3 A
Active power stays 40 kW; only Q and S change

items: Taking V × I as the power in watts; it is the apparent power in VA unless the pf is 1.
Adding kVA values of different loads arithmetically instead of adding P and Q separately.
Using peak values in VI cos φ: with V_m and I_m the average power is (V_m I_m/2) cos φ.
Forgetting that a capacitor's VAR output is 2πfCV², so it falls with the square of the voltage.
Over-sizing the correction bank so the net Q goes negative and the pf becomes leading.

theoryAdd.text: Keep these tan φ values ready for correction problems: pf 0.9 -> 0.484, 0.866 -> 0.577, 0.8 -> 0.75, 0.707 -> 1.0, 0.6 -> 1.333. Then Q = P tan φ and Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂) take seconds.

questions.questionText: Apparent power in an AC circuit is expressed in:
questions.explanation: Apparent power S = VI is the product of rms voltage and rms current, measured in VA (or kVA).

questions.questionText: A 200 V supply delivers 5 A to a load at a power factor of 0.6. The active power is:
questions.explanation: P = VI cos φ = 200 × 5 × 0.6 = 600 W. VI = 1000 VA is the apparent power, and 800 would be VI sin φ (in VAR).

questions.questionText: The instrument that directly measures the active power drawn by an AC load is the:
questions.explanation: A wattmeter responds to the product of voltage, current and the cosine of the angle between them, so it reads VI cos φ directly.

questions.questionText: A load draws an apparent power of 10 kVA and an active power of 6 kW. Its reactive power is:
questions.explanation: Q = √(S² − P²) = √(100 − 36) = 8 kVAR. Subtracting 10 − 6 = 4 or adding 6 + 10 are the usual slips.

questions.questionText: A load takes 12 kW of active power and 5 kVAR of reactive power. The apparent power is:
questions.explanation: S = √(P² + Q²) = √(144 + 25) = 13 kVA. Active and reactive powers are at right angles, so they cannot be added arithmetically.

questions.questionText: An induction motor running on load normally operates at:
questions.explanation: An induction motor needs magnetizing current, so it is an inductive load that draws current lagging the voltage (typically 0.7 to 0.9 lagging at full load).

questions.questionText: For a 50 Hz supply, the instantaneous power drawn by a single-phase load pulsates at:
questions.explanation: p = VI cos φ − VI cos(2ωt − φ), so the power varies at twice the supply frequency: 2 × 50 = 100 Hz.

questions.questionText: A current of 4 A flows through a series circuit with R = 10 Ω and impedance Z = 20 Ω. The active power is:
questions.explanation: Active power is dissipated only in the resistance: P = I²R = 4² × 10 = 160 W. I²Z = 320 is the apparent power in VA.

questions.questionText: A series circuit has R = 12 Ω and X_L = 5 Ω. Its power factor is approximately:
questions.explanation: Z = √(12² + 5²) = 13 Ω, so pf = R/Z = 12/13 ≈ 0.923, lagging because the reactance is inductive. 5/13 = 0.385 is sin φ.

questions.questionText: When a capacitor bank is connected in parallel with an inductive load to improve its power factor, the active power taken by the load:
questions.explanation: The capacitor only supplies reactive power; the load's voltage is unchanged, so it takes the same active power. Only the reactive power, apparent power and line current fall.

questions.questionText: A circuit in which the current leads the applied voltage is said to have:
options: A leading power factor, as in a capacitive load
A lagging power factor, as in a capacitive load
A leading power factor, as in an inductive load
A unity power factor, as in a resistive load
questions.explanation: The power factor is named after the current: when the current leads the voltage the pf is leading, which happens with a net capacitive load.

questions.questionText: Large power transformers and alternators are rated in kVA rather than kW because:
options: Their output is always at unity power factor
Their losses depend on voltage and current, not on the load power factor
kVA is always smaller than kW
questions.explanation: Copper loss depends on current and iron loss on voltage, so heating is set by VA. The manufacturer does not know the load pf, so the machine is rated in kVA.

questions.questionText: A load operates at a power factor of 0.8. Its reactive factor (sin φ) is:
questions.explanation: sin φ = √(1 − cos²φ) = √(1 − 0.64) = 0.6. The reactive factor is Q/S.

questions.questionText: A 230 V load draws 10 A at a power factor of 0.8 lagging. The reactive power is:
questions.explanation: sin φ = 0.6, so Q = VI sin φ = 230 × 10 × 0.6 = 1380 VAR. 1840 is VI cos φ, the active power in W.

questions.questionText: A single-phase load of 11.5 kW is supplied at 230 V with a power factor of 0.5. The line current is:
questions.explanation: I = P/(V cos φ) = 11 500/(230 × 0.5) = 100 A. At unity pf the same power would need only 50 A.

questions.questionText: A series circuit with R = 30 Ω and X_L = 40 Ω is connected to 200 V. The active power consumed is:
questions.explanation: Z = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω, I = 200/50 = 4 A, P = I²R = 16 × 30 = 480 W. 800 VA is the apparent power and 640 VAR the reactive power.

questions.questionText: A series circuit with R = 8 Ω and X_C = 6 Ω is connected to 100 V. The reactive power is:
questions.explanation: Z = √(8² + 6²) = 10 Ω, I = 10 A, Q = I²X_C = 100 × 6 = 600 VAR. The load is capacitive, so the reactive power is leading (supplied by the load).

questions.questionText: A 50 µF capacitor is connected to a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. The reactive power it supplies is approximately:
What capacitance is needed to supply 5 kVAR at 400 V, 50 Hz?
questions.explanation: C = Q_C/(2πfV²) = 5000/(2π × 50 × 400²) ≈ 99.5 µF. Leaving out 2π gives 625 µF.

questions.questionText: A 4 kW heater (unity pf) and a motor taking 3 kW at 0.6 pf lagging are supplied from the same source. The overall power factor is approximately:
questions.explanation: Motor Q = 3 × tan(cos⁻¹0.6) = 4 kVAR. Total P = 7 kW, Q = 4 kVAR, S = √(49 + 16) ≈ 8.06 kVA, so pf = 7/8.06 ≈ 0.87 lagging. Averaging the pfs (0.8) is wrong.

questions.questionText: A load draws 10 A (rms) from a 100 V (rms) supply with the current lagging by 60°. The minimum value of the instantaneous power is:
questions.explanation: p = VI cos φ − VI cos(2ωt − φ) swings between VI cos φ ± VI. P = 1000 × 0.5 = 500 W, so p_min = 500 − 1000 = −500 W: for part of each cycle energy flows back to the source.

questions.questionText: A wattmeter, voltmeter and ammeter connected to a single-phase load read 1200 W, 240 V and 8 A. The power factor of the load is:
A 100 kW load operates at 0.6 pf lagging. The capacitor kVAR needed to raise the power factor to unity is approximately:
questions.explanation: Q_C = P(tan φ₁ − tan φ₂) = 100 × (1.333 − 0) ≈ 133 kVAR. 167 kVA is the apparent power, and 80 kVAR (P sin φ) is not the load's reactive power.

questions.questionText: A 50 kW load has a power factor of 0.8 lagging. The capacitor kVAR required to improve the power factor to 0.95 lagging is approximately:
questions.explanation: tan φ₁ = 0.75 and tan φ₂ = tan(cos⁻¹0.95) ≈ 0.329, so Q_C = 50 × (0.75 − 0.329) ≈ 21.1 kVAR. 37.5 kVAR is the load's whole reactive power.

questions.questionText: For a fixed active power and supply voltage, the power factor of a load is improved from 0.6 to 0.9. The I²R loss in the supply cable falls to about what fraction of its original value?
questions.explanation: I ∝ 1/cos φ, so loss ∝ 1/cos²φ. New/old = (0.6/0.9)² = 0.444, about 44 %. 67 % is the ratio of the currents, not the losses.

questions.questionText: The voltage and current of a load are V = 100∠30° V and I = 5∠−15° A (rms). The active and reactive powers are approximately:
questions.explanation: S = V I* = (100∠30°)(5∠+15°) = 500∠45° VA = 354 + j354. Positive Q means an inductive (lagging) load; the current lags the voltage by 45°. Using I instead of I* gives the wrong angle 15°.

questions.questionText: The complex power of a load is S = P + jQ with P positive and Q negative. The load is:
options: Inductive, with a lagging power factor
Capacitive, with a leading power factor
questions.explanation: With S = V I*, a negative Q means the current leads the voltage, which is a capacitive load. The positive P shows it still absorbs active power.

questions.questionText: A workshop takes 45 kW at a power factor of 0.75 lagging from a 400 V single-phase supply. Its kVA demand and line current are:
questions.explanation: S = P/cos φ = 45/0.75 = 60 kVA and I = S/V = 60 000/400 = 150 A. Multiplying by the pf instead of dividing gives 33.8 kVA.

questions.questionText: A 500 kVA transformer is fully loaded. How much additional active power can it supply if the load power factor is raised from 0.7 to 0.9 at the same kVA?
questions.explanation: At 0.7 pf: P = 500 × 0.7 = 350 kW; at 0.9 pf: P = 450 kW. The extra capacity is 450 − 350 = 100 kW with no change in the transformer's current or kVA.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of a low power factor, for the same active power and voltage?
options: More active power is converted into useful work by the load
Larger copper losses in cables and transformers
questions.explanation: The load's active power is the same; a low pf raises the current, which increases I²R losses and voltage drop. It does not give the load more useful power.

questions.questionText: Besides static capacitors, which machine can supply leading reactive power for power-factor correction?
questions.explanation: An over-excited synchronous motor draws leading current, so it behaves like a capacitor; run without load for this purpose it is called a synchronous condenser.

questions.questionText: Power-factor correction in practice is usually stopped at about 0.95 rather than taken to exactly unity because:
options: Unity power factor would make the active power zero
Capacitors cannot supply reactive power at unity power factor
The line current increases as the power factor approaches unity
The capacitor kVAR needed rises steeply near unity for a small further reduction in current
questions.explanation: For 100 kW, going from 0.9 to 0.95 needs about 15.6 kVAR, but 0.95 to 1.0 needs about 32.9 kVAR for only about 5 % less current, so the last step is uneconomical; overshooting also gives a leading pf.

questions.questionText: A pure inductor with X_L = 46 Ω is connected to a 230 V supply. The active and reactive powers are:
questions.explanation: I = 230/46 = 5 A. A pure inductor dissipates no energy, so P = 0, and Q = I²X_L = 25 × 46 = 1150 VAR (lagging).

questions.questionText: A series RLC circuit with R = 10 Ω and X_L = X_C = 20 Ω is connected to 100 V. The reactive power absorbed by the inductor alone is:
questions.explanation: At X_L = X_C the circuit is resonant: I = V/R = 10 A, so Q_L = I²X_L = 100 × 20 = 2000 VAR. The capacitor supplies an equal 2000 VAR, so the net reactive power from the source is zero.

questions.questionText: A 50 Ω resistor and an inductor of reactance 25 Ω are connected in parallel across a 100 V supply. The power factor is approximately:
questions.explanation: P = V²/R = 200 W and Q = V²/X_L = 400 VAR, so pf = 200/√(200² + 400²) ≈ 0.447. Treating them as a series pair (R/Z = 50/55.9) wrongly gives 0.894.

questions.questionText: A 230 V, 50 Hz single-phase load takes 5 kW at 0.6 pf lagging. The parallel capacitance needed to raise the power factor to unity is approximately:
questions.explanation: Q_C = P tan φ₁ = 5000 × 1.333 = 6667 VAR; C = Q_C/(2πfV²) = 6667/(2π × 50 × 230²) ≈ 401 µF. Using Q = P (5 kVAR) instead gives about 301 µF, and Q = S (8.33 kVA) about 501 µF.

questions.questionText: A 10 kW single-phase load on 400 V operates at 0.707 pf lagging. After a capacitor raises the power factor to 0.9 lagging, the line current falls from about 35.4 A to about:
questions.explanation: I = P/(V cos φ): before, 10 000/(400 × 0.707) ≈ 35.4 A; after, 10 000/(400 × 0.9) ≈ 27.8 A. 25 A would be the current at unity pf.

questions.questionText: A 20 kW load at 0.8 pf lagging has a 25 kVAR capacitor bank connected across it. The resulting power factor is approximately:
questions.explanation: Load Q = 20 × 0.75 = 15 kVAR lagging; net Q = 15 − 25 = −10 kVAR (leading). pf = 20/√(20² + 10²) ≈ 0.894 leading: the bank over-corrects.

questions.questionText: A capacitor bank rated 10 kVAR at 415 V is operated at 380 V with the frequency unchanged. The reactive power it now supplies is approximately:
questions.explanation: Q_C = V²/X_C, so it scales with the square of the voltage: 10 × (380/415)² ≈ 8.38 kVAR. Scaling linearly gives 9.16 kVAR.

questions.questionText: A load has v = 200 sin(314t) V and i = 10 sin(314t − 60°) A. The average power consumed is:
questions.explanation: P = (V_m I_m/2) cos φ = (200 × 10/2) × cos 60° = 1000 × 0.5 = 500 W. Forgetting to convert peak values to rms gives 1000 W.

questions.questionText: A load takes 9 kW at 0.6 pf lagging. Its reactive power is:
questions.explanation: S = P/cos φ = 9/0.6 = 15 kVA, so Q = √(15² − 9²) = 12 kVAR (equivalently P tan φ = 9 × 4/3).

questions.questionText: Which statement about several loads connected to the same AC supply is correct?
options: Their apparent powers always add arithmetically to give the total kVA
Their active powers add, and their reactive powers add algebraically with capacitive VAR taken as negative
Their power factors add to give the overall power factor
Only the active powers add; reactive powers of different loads cannot be combined
questions.explanation: Total P = ΣP and total Q = ΣQ (inductive positive, capacitive negative); the total S = √(P² + Q²) is generally less than the arithmetic sum of the individual kVA.

questions.questionText: For a series RL circuit, which of the following expressions does NOT give the active power?
options: V_R²/R, where V_R is the voltage across R
questions.explanation: Active power is dissipated only in R: P = I²R = VI cos φ = V_R²/R. I²Z = VI is the apparent power in VA.

questions.questionText: Reactive power in an AC circuit represents:
options: Energy converted into heat in the resistance
Power lost permanently in the magnetic core
The peak value of the active power
Energy that flows back and forth between the source and the fields of L and C, with zero average value
questions.explanation: Reactive power measures the rate at which energy is stored and returned by inductors and capacitors each half-cycle; its average over a cycle is zero, so it does no net work.
